slides.title: Why Use Collections?
slides.content: Arrays have a fixed size set at creation. Collections grow and shrink automatically as you add and remove items, which is usually what you want.
slides.exampleOutput: list grows to hold 2 items; fixedSize stays length 3.

exercise.prompt: Which statement about arrays is TRUE?
options: The size can change after creation
The size is fixed at creation time
exercise.answer: The size is fixed at creation time

slides.title: Creating a List
slides.content: List<T> stores strongly-typed items you can index from 0. T is the element type, so a List<int> only accepts integers.

exercise.prompt: Complete the line to create an empty list of strings.

slides.title: List Methods
slides.content: Add appends one item, Remove removes the first match, Count is the number of items, and IndexOf returns an item's position (-1 if absent).

exercise.prompt: Complete the code so it prints the number of items in the list.
hints: Use the property that returns how many items are stored.
The property is named Count, just like Length on arrays.

slides.title: Iterating a List
slides.content: Use a foreach loop to read every element in order without managing an index.
slides.exampleOutput: Prints each value on its own line.

exercise.prompt: The loop that reads each element of a collection is a _____ loop.

slides.title: Dictionary<TKey, TValue>
slides.content: A Dictionary maps unique keys to values. Use it when you look something up by a key instead of by position.

exercise.prompt: Complete the line to declare a dictionary mapping strings to ints.

slides.title: Dictionary Access and Safety
slides.content: Reading a missing key throws KeyNotFoundException. Use ContainsKey first, or TryGetValue to get the value and a success flag safely.
slides.exampleOutput: Prints only when a value is present.

exercise.prompt: Complete the code so it prints the count only when the key exists.
hints: The method returns true when the key is found and outputs the value.
Use TryGetValue with an out variable, then print that variable.

slides.title: Choosing a Collection
slides.content: Use a List<T> when you access items by position. Use a Dictionary<TKey,TValue> when you look up by key. Both grow automatically and are type-safe.
slides.example:
var todo = new List<string>();            // ordered, by index
var byId = new Dictionary<int, string>();   // by key
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.
